web_title: 8. Stage 2 Technical Structure, Institutional Flow & Momentum Setup
question: Has Stallion stabilized since 13 November, or has the chart broken its last long-term structural floor?

epigraph.quote: Trading below both 50D SMA (204.15) and 200D/30W floor (183.54); trend is broken.
epigraph.author: Multi-timeframe TradingView tape assessment for NSE:STALLION, 25 November 2026 close [32]

web_blocks.html: Between 13 November and late November 2026, Stallion's chart moved from fragile to broken. On 13 November, the stock closed at ₹187.12, still 2.3% above its 200-day simple moving average. By the 23 November NSE market-facts ledger, Stallion fell to ₹180.48—below its ₹183.33 200-day average on 2.08 times normal volume, logging seven distribution days in 25 sessions [32]. Two sessions later, on 25 November live TradingView, sellers drove it down another 4.93% to ₹171.59 on 475,322 shares (1.55x 30-day average) [32]. The stock is now 38.5% below its ₹279.00 peak, down 23.6% over three months and 5.1% over six months [32].

In the Weinstein cycle, Stallion sits in a clear Stage 4 downtrend. The live TradingView evaluation marks it as Stage 4, flags a broken trend, and sets a hard rejection ceiling against new capital [32]. We label both dated feeds explicitly. The 23 November NSE ledger recorded ₹180.48 after an initial 200-day break, while the 25 November live close at ₹171.59 confirmed breakdown below every major average [32]. Both feeds show sellers in full control.
We map the 25 November live TradingView close of ₹171.59 against every daily, weekly, and 4-hour average, alongside 23 November NSE ledger benchmarks [32].

web_blocks.takeaway: Stallion has lost all eight tracked moving averages—including the 200-day simple average at ₹183.54—turning prior long-term support into overhead supply.

web_blocks.html: Momentum confirms active selling across all three timeframes. Weekly RSI stands at 42.09 on the 25 November live feed [32]. Daily RSI slid to 33.40, down from 38.33 on the 23 November ledger and 40.6 on 13 November [32]. Four-hour RSI fell to 27.53 [32]. Low RSI readings inside a Stage 4 break are not buy signals; they show heavy supply overwhelming weak bids. TradingView's composite rating is −0.60, with moving averages at −0.93 and oscillators at −0.27 [32]. Fourteen-day ATR is ₹10.05 (5.9% of price), while Bollinger Band width sits at 23.51%—showing downside expansion rather than quiet basing [32].

web_blocks.title: Peer tape comparison and the No-FOMO entry gate

web_blocks.html: Stallion's decline is stock-specific, not a sector selloff. On the same 25 November live snapshot, Gujarat Fluorochemicals (₹4,731.80) and Navin Fluorine (₹9,956.00) hold strong Stage 2 uptrends, up 28.0% and 37.4% over six months [34][35]. SRF (₹2,516.00) has rebuilt a Stage 1 base above its 50-day line [33]. The Nifty 50 also stays in an uptrend, with 55.2% of top-500 stocks above their 50-day lines. Stallion lags both peers and the index as buyers price in November's governance and capex shocks [32][36][37][38].
We test every No-FOMO gate against the 25 November live close of ₹171.59 and the 23 November NSE ledger close of ₹180.48 [32].

web_blocks.takeaway: Zero gates pass. Unlike 13 November when the 200-day average still held marginally, every single trend, momentum, volume, and fundamental gate now fails simultaneously.

web_blocks.html: At ₹171.59, price sits just 7.4% above the ₹155.07 to ₹159.79 pivot S1 shelf (centered at ₹157.43, structural floor ₹152.41) [32]. Approaching that shelf is no longer a buy trigger. Support works only when business quality holds and volume dries up. Here, down-day volume jumped on both 23 November (2.08x) and 25 November (1.55x), and our ₹143.2 FY28 base value sits below the entire shelf [32]. If ₹152.41 breaks on a weekly close, the next pivot sits at ₹130.89 (−23.7%), with the 52-week low at ₹99.32 [32].

web_blocks.title: Ownership flow decoded and derivatives status

web_blocks.html: Our 13 November draft could not explain why promoter stake fell 20.10 points between September 2025 and March 2026. Primary filings now prove both steps [15][40]. First, SEBI SAST records confirm CEO Shazad Rustomji sold 24,28,987 shares (3.06%) in the open market from 29 October to 4 November 2025 [40]. That cut promoter stake to 64.84%. Next, minimal promoter buying in the February 2026 rights issue diluted their stake another 17.04 points to 47.80% [15][36]. Meanwhile, combined institutional holding fell from 8.02% in March 2025 to 1.88% by September 2026 (0.28% FII, 1.60% DII) [15]. Public retail ownership crossed 50.33% across 66,734 accounts [15]. That shift leaves heavy trapped retail supply overhead.

Stallion is outside the NSE derivatives segment, so no listed options chain exists to hedge risk or track implied volatility. The multi-timeframe package flags a broken floor with zero 4-hour reversal [32]. Without desktop browser automation in this environment, the chart readout uses public NSE and TradingView technical feeds strictly [32].

web_blocks.title: What technical repair would actually look like

web_blocks.html: A quick oversold bounce from ₹157 or ₹171 will not repair this chart. Stallion must first stop making lower lows and build a quiet multi-week Stage 1 base with light down-day volume. It then needs to reclaim its 4-hour 20-period average (₹182.61) and 200-day average (₹183.54) [32]. Finally, it must post weekly closes above a flattening 30-week average (₹202.66) and 50-day average (₹204.15) on strong volume [32]. Until that repair aligns with audited operational proof, treat rallies as bounces inside a Stage 4 decline.

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
paragraphs: Price often reflects governance and execution leaks before investors finish reading the footnotes. Stallion broke its 200-day line on heavy volume in the same week Navin Fluorine and Gujarat Fluorochemicals held Stage 2 highs. That relative weakness is a clear warning.
When shares move from promoters and funds into 66,000 retail accounts ahead of a third fundraise, overhead supply builds fast. Respect the Stage 4 tape and wait for real basing plus audited proof.

book_paragraphs: Now let us read the tape, and let us be completely candid about what changed in just twelve days between 13 November and 25 November 2026. In our prior edition, Stallion closed at 187.12 rupees and still clung 2.3% above its 200-day simple moving average. That single line was the last structural support standing between a messy pullback and an outright Stage 4 breakdown. By late November, that last line broke cleanly.

Keep the two verified session dates straight so the timeline is crystal clear. On the 23 November 2026 NSE market-facts ledger, Stallion closed at 180.48 rupees, already slipping beneath its 200-day average of 183.33 rupees on more than double its 20-day average volume, and accumulating seven distribution days inside twenty-five sessions. Two trading sessions later, at the 25 November 2026 live TradingView close, the stock fell another 4.93% to 171.59 rupees on 475,322 shares—1.55 times its 30-day average volume. Stallion is now 38.5% below its 52-week high of 279 rupees, down 23.6% over three months, and down 5.1% over six months.

In Stan Weinstein's four-stage market cycle, this is an unambiguous Stage 4 downtrend. Every single moving average we track now sits above the share price as overhead resistance. The 10-day simple average sits at 183.58 rupees, 6.5% above the close. The 20-day average sits at 189.27 rupees, 9.3% overhead. The 50-day average has rolled over sharply to 204.15 rupees—nearly 16% above price—down from 220.46 rupees just a month earlier. Most importantly, the 200-day simple moving average at 183.54 rupees is now 6.5% above the stock, and the 30-week simple moving average—the classic Stage 2 dividing line—sits 15.3% overhead at 202.66 rupees. Both the 10-week and 40-week exponential averages have also turned into ceilings at 194.39 and 189.17 rupees.

Check the multi-timeframe momentum readings and you see the exact same story across weekly, daily, and four-hour bars. Weekly RSI sits at 42.09, confirming medium-term sellers remain in charge. Daily RSI has dropped to 33.40, down from 40.6 two weeks earlier. On the 4-hour chart—the shortest timeframe we inspect to see whether buyers are stepping in to defend a shelf—RSI has sunk to 27.53 while the close of 171.59 rupees sits six percent below the 4-hour 20-period exponential average of 182.61 rupees. Some traders get excited whenever an RSI drops below 30 and call it oversold. In a confirmed Stage 4 downtrend, oversold readings are not a floor; they are a warning that persistent sellers are overwhelming weak bids.

Volatility confirms the direction of pressure. Fourteen-day average true range is 10.05 rupees, nearly six percent of the share price on an ordinary day, and Bollinger Band width has expanded to 23.51%. Healthy stocks building a launchpad contract in volatility as weak hands finish selling and quiet accumulation begins. Stallion is doing the opposite: bands are widening downward on above-average down-day volume.

What makes this breakdown doubly damning is the comparison against its own industry peers on the very same trading day. You cannot blame the broader Indian market, because the Nifty 50 remains in an uptrend with more than half of the top 500 stocks trading above their 50-day moving averages. And you cannot blame the fluorochemical sector either. On the 25 November live TradingView snapshot, Gujarat Fluorochemicals sits in a confirmed Stage 2 uptrend at 4,731.80 rupees, up 28% over six months and just 5.7% off its 52-week high. Navin Fluorine sits in a powerful Stage 2 uptrend at 9,956 rupees, up 37.4% over six months and less than 4% off its high. Even SRF, which had been lagging earlier in November, has repaired into a Stage 1 base at 2,516 rupees, back above its 50-day average. Stallion is falling alone because investors are repricing Stallion's own operational delays, negative cash flow, and governance flags.

Ownership flow explains why rallies in Stallion face such heavy resistance. In our prior edition, we noted that promoter ownership fell from 67.90% in September 2025 to 47.80% in March 2026, but we could not verify how it happened. Now we have the primary filings. SEBI SAST disclosures prove that Chairman and CEO Shazad Rustomji sold 24.29 lakh shares—3.06% of the company—in the open market across four sessions in late October and early November 2025. Then, during the February 2026 rights issue, minimal promoter participation diluted their stake by another 17.04 percentage points. Over the same stretch, institutional investors largely walked away: combined foreign and domestic institutional ownership shrank from 8.02% in March 2025 to just 1.88% by September 2026. Public retail ownership jumped past 50.33% across 66,734 accounts.

Think about the market mechanics of that shareholder register. When a stock transitions from concentrated promoter and institutional hands into tens of thousands of retail accounts—and then drops 38.5% from its peak—every bounce toward 185, 195, or 205 rupees runs straight into trapped retail holders eager to get back to breakeven. Combine that trapped overhead supply with management signaling another 200 crore capital raise, and you understand why institutional demand is absent.

Now consider the support zone we highlighted in our prior dossier: 155.07 to 159.79 rupees, centered on the classic first pivot at 157.43 rupees, with a structural invalidation stop at 152.41 rupees. At 171.59 rupees, the stock is now only 7.4% above the top of that shelf. Why do we not keep waiting patiently to buy at 159 rupees? Because technical support is never an automatic buy order when the fundamentals and governance beneath the chart have failed. A support shelf is simply a place where buyers showed up in the past. When a company misses two plant deadlines, turns cash-flow negative, receives a monitoring-agency qualification for fund deviation and commingling, and sees its base fair value drop to 143.2 rupees—below the entire support shelf—buying a falling knife at 159 rupees is poor discipline. If 152.41 breaks on a weekly close, the next technical pivot sits at 130.89 rupees, nearly 24% lower, with the 52-week low down at 99.32 rupees.

Finally, a brief note on derivatives. Stallion is not included in the NSE futures and options segment, so there is no liquid options chain to structure a defined-risk call spread or inspect implied volatility. Any exposure to Stallion is strictly unhedged cash equity, which raises the bar for both business quality and technical structure. Neither bar is close to met today.

So what would it take for the tape to earn a second look? Not a one-day dead-cat bounce from oversold RSI. Stallion would first need to stop making lower lows, spend weeks carving a calm Stage 1 base with drying down-day volume, reclaim its 200-day average at 183.54 rupees, and break out decisively above a flattening 30-week average near 203 rupees on strong institutional-grade volume—all alongside audited evidence that Bhilwara is producing commercial R-32 and cash conversion has turned positive. Until then, the tape confirms what the financials and valuation already proved: stay away. Chapter 9 pulls both sides of the aisle together and sets out the final hard-rejection decision.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: When two direct competitors hit Stage 2 highs in the exact same week your stock breaks its 200-day average on heavy volume, listen to the market. Relative weakness is rarely random, and buying a Stage 4 breakdown ahead of a third capital raise is a lesson you do not need to pay tuition to learn.
